claims.text: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by a balance between configurational mixing entropy and element-specific pairwise interaction energies.
Interactions involving Al make especially important contributions to phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
The initial high-temperature Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 material is a metastable BCC phase.
Cooling lowers the configurational-entropy contribution to phase stability.
DFT-derived pairwise interactions can provide predictive features for phase formation in multicomponent alloys.
Local atomic ordering and clustering in this alloy are dictated by the strengths of constituent-element pairwise interactions.
At high temperature, configurational entropy overcomes attractive pair interactions and stabilizes a single-phase BCC state.
On cooling, favorable binary interactions drive chemical ordering and clustering.
Interaction-driven chemical ordering and clustering nucleate secondary phases.
Slower cooling promotes more pronounced ordering than rapid cooling.
Slow cooling will produce measurable ordered clusters, precipitates, or secondary phases.
Ordered clusters or secondary phases will be absent or significantly reduced after rapid quenching relative to slow cooling.
The high-temperature baseline is a single-phase BCC structure stabilized by mixing entropy.
Approximately 7 at.% Al is sufficient to alter local chemical interactions without dominating lattice stability.
The proposed mechanism applies below a critical temperature at which configurational entropy has declined sufficiently.
Kinetic constraints during cooling can alter the extent of ordering independently of the thermodynamic driving force.
Slow cooling and rapid quenching constitute the controlled comparison used to test the proposed cooling-rate dependence.
Similar single-phase BCC structures with no greater ordering or clustering after slow cooling would falsify the proposed mechanism.
